source: Holyoak and Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction. JEP:General 128(1):3-31, Experiment 1
finding: Students rated six points of dispute in a Quest v. Smith libel case before the case (pretest), then read it and gave a verdict. Ratings moved toward the verdict. In the 3-phase condition most of the shift was already there at an interim test before the verdict was committed.
numbers: N=54 UCLA undergraduates (24 two-phase, 30 three-phase); 6 three-phase 'switchers' excluded, 48 analysed. Verdicts 26 Quest, 22 Smith. Verdict x test interaction F(1,44)=35.3, p<.001. Mean Q-score pretest .37 (Quest) vs -.20 (Smith), p=.06; posttest 1.42 vs -1.56, p<.001. Three-phase: F(2,44)=11.2, p<.001; interim and posttest did not differ (p>.20). 75% of participants rated confidence 4-5 of 5. Pretest was a separate booklet followed by a 3-5 min unrelated task, same session.
quote: Assessments of the individual arguments shifted so as to cohere with their emerging verdict.
limits: No effect size reported in the paper (only F and p). Pretest already leaned toward verdict at p=.06; one pretest item (regulate the Internet) predicted verdict. Switchers (6 of 30, 20%) were dropped and did not show the pattern. Pretest was in the same session, so this does not test a separate-session baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: gives the founding numbers. Rating drift happens before the verdict is stated, so a pre-commit rating taken in the same context is not clean.

source: Holyoak and Simon (1999) JEP:General, Experiment 2 (1-week delay, memory for pretest)
finding: Small replication with the pretest in a separate session one week before the case. The coherence shift persisted. A third session showed recalled pretest ratings were pulled toward the verdict.
numbers: N=19 UCLA upper-division students (9 Quest, 10 Smith), three sessions one week apart, five points of dispute. Pretest Q -.34 vs -.30; posttest .94 vs -1.03; verdict x test F(1,17)=7.71, p=.01. Recall of pretest: best predictor was verdict r(16)=.43, p=.07 (not reliable).
limits: N=19, volunteers in a lab course, tested by a classmate. Memory-bias effect only marginal. Pretest was a quick 10 min booklet, so ratings may be shallow.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 answer: yes, the shift survives a separate pretest session in humans (small N). The LLM analogue (a fresh context holding only the pre-rating) has never been run.

source: Holyoak and Simon (1999) JEP:General, Experiment 3 (character manipulation, spreading to a second case)
finding: Telling participants the defendant had bad or good character shifted ratings on points barely linked to character. Coherence then spread to a second, different case (Infoscience) via a shared analogy.
numbers: N=80 (32 per condition, 16 baseline). Quest case: Q-score .93 (Bad Smith) vs -.71 (Good Smith); reliable (p<.01) for Truth and Cause, not for Analogy (p=.12) or Speech (p=.28). Analogy ratings: pretest r(62)=-.14, posttest r(62)=-.42. Infoscience case: verdict x test F(1,78)=36.4, p<.001; posttest Q-score 1.19 vs -1.52. Analogy-Credit correlation r(76)=.10 pretest vs .42 posttest.
limits: Spread to indirectly linked points was only partial (two of four significant). Structural-equation comparisons of credibility models are model-dependent.
agent_relevance: Shows spreading activation across linked claims, the same mechanism a graph solver uses. It also shows how one planted fact (character) can bias unrelated ratings, the failure to guard against.

source: Simon, Pham, Le and Holyoak (2001) The emergence of coherence over the course of decision making. JEP:Learning, Memory, Cognition 27(5):1250-1260, Experiment 1
finding: Replicates Holyoak and Simon with a leaning-first v leaning-second manipulation. The interim coherence shift occurred whether or not people had been asked to state a leaning, so the shift is not caused by stating a preliminary decision.
numbers: N=50 UCLA undergraduates (47 analysed after 3 switchers dropped); 49% final verdicts for Quest. Verdict x test F(2,86)=35.3, MSE=27.9, p<.0001. Baseline Q .39 vs -.41 (diff .80, F(1,43)=6.70, p=.01), interim diff 2.23, postdecision diff 2.55 (p<.001); interim to post shift not significant (p>.30). Leaning order x shift F(2,86)<1. 93% rated confidence high despite an even split.
limits: Baseline difference of .80 already present and significant, so part of the final gap is pre-existing preference. Baseline taken in same session. Same lab and same Quest case, so not an independent group.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: baseline diff .80 vs final diff 2.55 means about two thirds of the final spread is shift. Measure agent drift the same way, subtracting the baseline gap.

source: Simon, Pham, Le and Holyoak (2001) JEP:LMC, Experiments 2 and 3 (memorise, comprehend, communicate)
finding: The shift also appeared when participants were told to memorise the case (Exp 2) or to comprehend it (Exp 3), with no decision task. So coherence building is a general comprehension process, not only post-decision dissonance.
numbers: Exp 2: N=125 UCLA undergraduates, verdict x test F(2,236)=59.1, MSE=2.92, p<.0001. Exp 3: N=166, 9 switchers, verdict x test F(2,302)=78.6, MSE=2.92, p<.0001; shift also varied across six points, F(10,1510)=4.42. Exp 3 also had reception and communication conditions (transmitters showed larger coherence than receivers).
limits: 'Verdict' groups in no-decision conditions were defined by a later verdict, so a hidden leaning cannot be ruled out. Effect sizes not given. Same lab.
agent_relevance: Reading and summarising a case can bend ratings. An agent that summarises first and then rates is already inside the shift.

source: Qiao, Kamper, Lagnado and Holyoak (2026) Coherence and Bayesian reasoning in legal judgment: how verdicts reshape evidence evaluation. Proc. CogSci 48
finding: New-sample conceptual replication with an online sample and a mock burglary case. Agreement ratings with prosecution and defence arguments shifted toward the verdict (replicating Holyoak and Simon). But when argument strength was measured as a likelihood ratio, shifts were not aligned with verdicts.
numbers: Three studies, N=339 (Prolific). Study 1 N=130 (74 guilty, 56 not guilty): Verdict x Test x Side F(1,128)=96.31, p<.001; posttest prosecution agreement .80 (guilty) vs .53, defence .72 (not guilty) vs .42; pretest no difference (p>.119). Studies 2a (N=126) and 2b (N=83, 82 analysed): log-LR Verdict x Test F(1,124)=5.10, p=.026 and F(1,81)=4.98, p=.028; three-way interaction p=.083 and p=.44; general fall in diagnosticity of both sides.
quote: These results replicate those of Holyoak and Simon (1999)
limits: Pretest and posttest in one session. Pretest items were generic and posttest items case-specific, so wording differs. Conference paper. Study 2 did not show verdict-aligned shifts in the normative measure. Causal direction unresolved. Holyoak is a co-author, so not fully independent.
agent_relevance: The shift is real in agreement ratings but weak in probability-like ratings. If our agent rates evidence as likelihood ratios in a structured form, drift may be smaller than free-text agreement suggests.

source: Qiao et al. (2026) CogSci 48, constraint satisfaction network and Bayesian network modelling
finding: A constraint satisfaction network (conditional probabilities, agreements, verdict nodes) predicted the mean pre-to-post shifts, with coherence flowing from verdict to agreement but not strongly back to likelihoods. A Bayesian network fitted to post-verdict estimates reproduced guilt judgments. The authors treat the two as compatible, not rivals.
numbers: CSN predicted 48 values; r=.87 for P(A|G), r=.79 for P(A|not G), r=.86 for agreement, all p<.001, RMSE .080-.093. A model with bidirectional links between likelihood and agreement fit substantially worse. BN built from N=204 (107 guilty, 97 not guilty).
limits: Fit is to group means on 16 points per measure with free parameters (overfit risk). BN parameters partly from a pilot (N=30) and flagged by the authors as possibly artefactual.
agent_relevance: Supports a mixed design: a solver for settling, a probability layer for the final number. Not a test of ECHO itself.

source: Huntsman and Thomas (2025) Benchmarking graph construction by large language models for coherence-driven inference (arXiv 2502.13953v2)
finding: Benchmark of how well LLMs rebuild a signed coherence graph from natural-language propositions made to instantiate a known graph. Reasoning models do best; one prompt suffices for sparse graphs. This closes the title-only lead a31.
numbers: 76 synthetic Erdos-Renyi graphs (38 sparse, 38 dense), 5-23 propositions each; median edge density .202 sparse and .734 dense. Models: o1-mini, o3-mini, o4-mini, QwQ-32B, Sky-T1-32B, phi-4, gemini-2.0-flash-exp, claude-3.5-sonnet, gpt-4o, llama-3.3-70B, llama-4-scout, gemini-1.5-pro. o1/3/4-mini reach perfect reconstruction about half the time on sparse graphs; o1/3/4-mini, claude-3.5-sonnet and QwQ-32B beat the rest on both densities (micro F1). Adding numeric uncertainty to propositions did not lower fidelity.
quote: o1/3/4-mini achieve perfect reconstruction half of the time on sparse graphs.
limits: Synthetic propositions with a known graph, not real legal evidence; one reconstruction per graph, no repeat-build variance reported. On real example graphs a degree test rejects the ER hypothesis (p about .001) for some, so benchmark topology is not realistic. GPT-5 and newer not tested. Authors say o3/4-mini are better on harder real instances but give no numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly closed: reconstruction fidelity is good but not perfect (half of sparse graphs exact), and dense graphs are worse. Real-case intercoder reliability across builds is still unmeasured.

source: Huntsman and Thomas (2025) arXiv 2502.13953v2, limits and recommendation
finding: The paper's own stated gaps: weights, topology realism and prompt strategy are left open. It frames coherence maximisation as MAX-CUT (APX-complete) on the signed graph and suggests a coherence theory of truth anchored by hard-coded established propositions.
numbers: No variance-across-builds statistic. Edge density target .15 sparse; node counts 5-23.
quote: our results indicate that it is now feasible to computationally instantiate a coherence theory of truth
limits: Feasibility argument, not an accuracy result on verdicts. Industry-lab preprint, not peer reviewed in this version.
agent_relevance: Practical rule: anchor the graph with data nodes that cannot be rejected (ECHO's special unit) and rebuild the graph two or three times, keeping edges that recur.

source: Singh, Cassel, Weir, Feng and Bayless (2026) VERGE: formal refinement and guidance engine for verifiable LLM reasoning (arXiv 2601.20055v3)
finding: LLM claims are checked by an SMT solver and the solver's minimal correction subsets (MCS) guide refinement. Compared with chain of thought (CoT), self-consistency (SC, k=3) and neuro-symbolic baselines on GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B and Claude 3.7 Sonnet. The solver-guided loop wins five of six benchmarks; the specialised Proof-of-Thought method wins ProofWriter.
numbers: Table 1, 5 runs each. Sonnet-3.7 FOLIO: CoT 70.4, SC 72.4, Logic-LM 71.6, VERGE 87.9. Sonnet-3.7 ProofWriter: CoT 71.6, SC 86.6, PoT 98.2, VERGE 93.0. GPT-OSS-120B FOLIO CoT 32.0, SC 35.5, VERGE 84.7 (low CoT baselines look like format failures). GPT-120B ZebraLogic CoT 84.0, SC 77.8, VERGE 91.0. AR-LSAT GPT-120B CoT 87.8, SC 88.7, VERGE 91.7. HLE GPT-OSS-120B 14.2 (CoT) to 30.5. Ablation GPT-120B: soft-only (no solver) ZebraLogic 70.2 vs full 91.0; no MCS on AR-LSAT 83.0 vs 91.7. Average gain at convergence 18.7%.
limits: This is SMT entailment checking with repair, not a coherence (MaxSAT over soft claims) solver. VERGE vs SC k=3 cost described only as 'comparable budgets', not equalised in the text I read. Some baselines (CoT 32.0 on FOLIO) look under-tuned. Models are 2025-26 mid-frontier, not top models. Preprint, v3.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: first 2025-26 evidence that a code-run solver over LLM-built claims beats SC and CoT on frontier-ish models, but only on formal-logic tasks, and not a coherence solver on legal evidence.

source: Singh et al. (2026) VERGE, formalisation fidelity and the formalisation barrier
finding: The solver is only as good as the translation into logic. Small models cannot translate; larger ones can but still err silently. Cross-model agreement is a usable alarm.
numbers: GPT-OSS-20B only about 30% valid SMT syntax; GPT-OSS-120B and Sonnet over 90%. FOLIO released gold formulas agree with dataset labels on only 72.6% of examples. Unanimous formalisations: fidelity 76.7% on FOLIO vs 56.0% non-unanimous (Fisher p=.002); 23.3% of unanimous FOLIO formalisations still disagree with gold. Errors are mostly conservative (91.9% on FOLIO give 'Uncertain'; 3.0% false assertions). FOLIO consensus: 29.1% unanimous, 31.5% majority, 39.4% none. Cross-family disagreement detects 94.1% of wrong formalisations at 28.8% precision. Z3 time is 0.25% of runtime; LLM sampling dominates.
limits: FOLIO and ProofWriter only; legal text is vaguer than FOLIO. Fidelity measured against gold formulas that are themselves wrong 27% of the time.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the formalisation-failure rate is the number to log. Plan for a quarter to a half of formalisations to be unreliable on real text; route to CoT when models disagree.

source: Kassner, Tafjord, Sabharwal, Richardson, Schuetze and Clark (2023) Language models with rationality (REFLEX), EMNLP; arXiv 2305.14250
finding: A MaxSAT (RC2) rational layer over an LLM's own answers, rules and negations. It flips true/false labels or rejects rules at minimum cost. Consistency rises sharply; accuracy stays flat. The failure analysis is the nearest thing to an error profile for solver flips.
numbers: Consistency (LLM to LLM+layer): EntailmentBank 87.0 to 96.1, OBQA 88.2 to 95.9, QuaRTz 85.7 to 96.6 (8-11 points). Accuracy: 79.4 to 79.9, 74.0 to 75.0, 80.2 to 80.0. Test sets 339, 500, 784 questions. Consistency ablation on EntailmentBank dev: dropping each rule type lowers it (to between 90.4 and 95.8; per-rule order garbled in my text extract). Manual analysis of 50 wrong EntailmentBank answers: missing rules 30%, incorrect beliefs not corrected 30%, ambiguous statements 10%, multiple valid answers 10%, bad rules 10% (categories overlap).
limits: Macaw-type 2022-era model, not frontier. Net accuracy change (+0.5, +1.0, -0.2) hides flips in both directions; no flip-to-wrong rate reported. Failure analysis covers only questions that ended wrong.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no flip-to-wrong rate exists even in the best study. Flat accuracy with an 8-11 point consistency gain means correct and incorrect flips roughly cancel. Consistency does not imply accuracy.

source: Ambati (2026) Certified coherent reasoning for LLMs via weighted MaxSAT and belief-revision geometry. ICLR 2026 Workshop on Logical Reasoning of LLMs
finding: Frames multi-query answering as picking the highest total preference answer set that is satisfiable. Compiles to weighted partial MaxSAT with checkable certificates. Defines a 'coherence gap' (log-preference sacrificed) and a minimal-change repair distance.
numbers: No empirical numbers on the page; proposes benchmark templates only. Notes NP-hardness under severe restrictions.
limits: Workshop abstract page only; no results, so it is not a test of solver vs majority vote.
agent_relevance: Useful metric to copy: the coherence gap says how much model confidence the solver overruled. Large gaps should flag a case for review.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence, BBS 12(3), Author's Response to commentators (Achinstein, Dawes, Klayman and Hogarth, Papineau, Lycan, McCauley, Chi, Earle)
finding: Concessions and replies. (1) Agrees with Klayman and Hogarth that his ECHO analyses do not constitute good tests of psychological validity; controlled experiments are needed. (2) Handles Dawes's Simpson-paradox challenge by adding an alternative hypothesis (Mike's two contradictory alibis), not by changing ECHO. (3) Papineau: use probabilities when available, but they rarely are for qualitative theory choice; calls his own position 'weak explanationist'. (4) McCauley on arbitrary inputs: expects disputants to agree on what explains what. (5) Earle: warns of input representation and free parameters.
numbers: No new numbers; the Mike alibi example is a worked ECHO input.
quote: the ECHO analyses presented in the target article do not constitute good tests of the psychological validity
limits: Author's own reading of critics. The Dawes example is a toy network, not data. The reply on arbitrary inputs is only an expectation.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 first half closed. The author concedes the input-coding and free-parameter problem, which supports blind graph rebuilds.

source: Thagard (1989) BBS 12(3), section 9.3 and reply on Ranney and Thagard (1988)
finding: The only human-data check of ECHO in the target article is Ranney and Thagard (1988): ECHO simulated two cases of belief revision in students learning naive physics, with propositions and links read from verbal protocols. The target text says the simulations captured the dynamics of belief change well; in reply Thagard calls this only the beginning of a series of experiments.
numbers: Two simulated cases; no correlation or fit statistic in the target article. The Ranney and Thagard (1988) DTIC report returned 403; Schank and Ranney and Read and Marcus-Newhall not found in open text.
quote: Ranney and Thagard (1988) is just the beginning of what I hope will be a series of experiments
limits: Not independent (Thagard is co-author). Qualitative fit to two protocols. Independent replications named from memory were not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 second half stays open: no independently opened replication of ECHO on human confidence data. Do not cite ECHO as validated on human data.

source: Cummins, Elson and Hussey (2025) Cognitive dissonance in large language models is neither cognitive nor dissonant (PsyArXiv 3ny67_v1)
finding: Re-ran the Lehr et al. Putin-essay dissonance paradigm with authorship varied: the model writes the essay v the essay is supplied in the user message. Essay valence shifted GPT-4o's Putin rating in every condition, so a model-authored (free choice) essay is not needed.
numbers: Three studies: Study 1 chat interface; Study 2 API; Study 3 one monologue with all text tagged as model- or user-authored. Valence effect in all. Sample sizes and effect sizes are not stated in the two-page commentary (figure shows 95% CIs only).
quote: All tokenised text, independent of authorship, becomes part of the context window and will influence the model's output.
limits: Commentary, not peer reviewed in this form. Authorship varied with identical essay content, which answers the design question, but no N or choice-vs-no-choice contrast is shown, so Lehr's d=0.98 choice moderation is not directly tested. One model, one topic.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the context-window account survives for the valence effect. Assume anything earlier in the context, by anyone, pulls later ratings; rate in a fresh context.

source: Search record for gaps 2, 5 and 8 (web search 2026-11-10 plus API attempts)
finding: No study was found that gives an LLM legal evidence, takes ratings, elicits a verdict, then re-rates in the same versus a fresh context (gap 2). No study was found comparing LLM-judged, NLI and gold links on a current model (gap 5). Koscholke and Jekel (2016, Synthese, DOI 10.1007/s11229-015-0996-6) tests probabilistic coherence measures psychologically but was paywalled and not opened (gap 8).
numbers: No numbers. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv API were rate-limited; Springer redirected to a login.
limits: Absence of results is search-limited (about 8 searches), not proof. Bovens-Hartmann and Olsson tests against ECHO on multiple testimony remain unread.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2, 5 and 8 stay open. Gap 2 is cheapest to run ourselves: same case, rate then verdict then re-rate, same context v fresh context.
